analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and their spouses from owning or trading individual stocks.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in November 2023 with zero cosponsors, sat in committee without a markup or vote until the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal ethics law to prohibit members of Congress and their spouses from buying or selling individual stocks and other securities. It allows them to keep broad investments like Treasury bonds, exchange-traded funds, mutual funds, and government retirement plans, so they could stay invested without picking individual companies. Members who break the rule would face a fine of at least $25,000 per violation, or the full value of the trade, whichever is higher, and compliance certificates would be published online each year.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, who would no longer face the conflict of interest created when the people who write laws and oversee industries can also buy and sell stock in the companies those decisions affect. Ethical members of both parties would also benefit from a clear, enforceable rule.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters worried about congressional conflicts of interest

how_it_helps.text: Bars members of Congress and their spouses from buying or selling securities (individual stocks), effective on enactment or when they take office, whichever is later.

Preserves broad, diversified holdings by excluding Treasury bills, notes, and bonds, exchange-traded funds, mutual funds, and government retirement plans from the ban, so members are not forced out of investing entirely.
Requires a pledge of compliance to the supervising ethics office and annual publication of compliance certificates on a public website, making adherence verifiable by anyone.
Sets a penalty of the greater of $25,000 per violation or the full value of the traded instrument, a penalty that scales with the size of the trade rather than being a fixed slap on the wrist.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their spouses who currently hold individual stocks would have to sell them and shift into broad funds or Treasury securities. Members whose spouses work in fields that pay in stock would lose some household income flexibility.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress holding individual stocks

drawbacks.text: The exemptions for exchange-traded funds and mutual funds leave a sizable channel: a member could hold a broad fund that is heavily weighted toward companies in industries they regulate, and the bill does nothing about that indirect exposure.

The spouse provision contains an exception: after one year in their primary occupation, a member's spouse may keep receiving stock as job compensation, which could allow ongoing household exposure to individual companies.

Enforcement depends entirely on the supervising ethics office identifying violations and members self-reporting compliance materials; the bill creates no independent watchdog or automatic trade-detection mechanism.

A good-faith objection is that an outright ownership ban may be broader than needed, since existing disclosure and trading-delay rules could address conflicts without barring members from all individual securities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit—removing the conflict when lawmakers trade stock in companies their decisions move—is real and the cost to members is modest, since diversified funds and Treasuries remain available. The design flaws (fund exemptions, the spouse compensation exception, ethics-office-only enforcement) keep it from being airtight, but the trade-off favors the public. Its fatal weakness was political: it attracted no cosponsors and never got a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Administration Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress expired.

narrative.text: Representative Pat Fallon, a Republican from Texas, introduced the Insider Trading Prevention Act on November 1, 2023.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on House Administration the same day, and that referral is the last action in its history — no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor from either party.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died in committee without a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress who hold or trade individual stocks came out ahead: they keep their current ability to buy and sell securities, subject only to existing disclosure rules, and no new restrictions or fines took effect. Voters gained nothing from this outcome.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress with stock portfolios

for.name: Pat Fallon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee, but recruited no cosponsors and did not pursue discharge or other routes to a floor vote.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration (chaired by Rep. Bryan Steil)
against.role: Committee of referral; controlled whether the bill got a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — leaving it to die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote to break down; the only support on record was a single Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and their spouses with individual stock portfolios
industries.note: The bill would require these officeholders to divest individual securities and face fines up to the full value of a violating trade. Their interest in keeping the status quo runs directly against the transparency the bill would provide voters, and nothing in the record forced them to give it up.
